nyc_001: You can recognise it as one of the oldest trees on Manhattan, standing at the northwest corner of the park. It stands at Washington Square Park.
nyc_003: You can recognise it by its low, twisted, weeping canopy, propped and cabled, spreading wide enough that you duck to walk beneath it. It stands near the Boathouse in Prospect Park, Brooklyn.
nyc_004: You can recognise it by its pair of trunks standing a few feet apart, likely survivors of one older root system. It stands in Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn.
nyc_005: You can recognise it by its height, 133.8 feet, the tallest carefully measured tree in New York City, rising from uncleared forest. It stands in Alley Pond Park, Queens.
nyc_006: You can recognise it by standing alone 75 feet north of the restroom beside the tennis courts, a leftover from a 19th century tree nursery. It stands in Kissena Park, Flushing, Queens.
nyc_007: You can recognise it by its trunk, 21.4 feet around, dwarfing everything nearby along the paved path. It stands at the north end of Clove Lakes Park, Staten Island.
nyc_008: You can recognise it as one of 144 evergreens planted around the glacial boulder called Sugar Loaf Rock, each marking a fallen soldier. It stands in Hero Park, Staten Island.
nyc_010: You can recognise it by its size, nearly 88 feet tall with a trunk over 3 feet across, standing on the east lawn. It stands beside the Van Cortlandt House Museum, the Bronx.
nyc_011: You can recognise it by being wider than it is tall, just under 51 feet high with a 55 foot canopy, right at the park's edge. It stands at Central Park West and 77th Street.
nyc_014: You can recognise it by its limbs arching downward and tangling into a low dark dome you duck into rather than stand under. It stands in Green-Wood Cemetery, at Garden Path and Pink Avenue.
